title: Neurodiverg-Ent
content: As entomologists, we study organisms representing a tremendous level of diversity. Humans are also incredibly diverse in many ways, including differences in the ways we think, feel, and learn. Unsurprisingly, these differences exist among entomologists, with many Entomological Society of America (ESA) members identifying as neurologically atypical, or neurodivergent. In a 2021 Psyche article, autistic author and Austrian entomologist Alice Laciny, Ph.D., proposed a few reasons why entomology appeals to neurodiverse individuals: arthropods provide sensory stimulation through their vast array of colors and structures; taxonomy and systematics provide an engaging challenge; and working with insects invokes a sense of camaraderie with the “weird.” Indeed, for many of us who were considered “weird kids” and felt alienated because we didn’t behave “as we should,” a need for belonging and companionship endeared us to misunderstood animals. Unfortunately, neurodivergent entomologists often feel alienated or judged within work spaces, and the infrastructure of academia poses unique challenges to neurodivergent individuals. This results in neurodivergent individuals either consciously or unconsciously suppressing and masking traits or hiding work-related struggles to prove that we belong in our field.
